title: Scheduled Task/Job: Container Orchestration Job
summary: This sub-technique is scheduled execution inside a container orchestration platform, where the scheduler is an object in the cluster's own database rather than a file on one host. In Kubernetes an operator writes a CronJob, which the controller turns into Job objects on a timetable, and each Job creates one or more pods that the scheduler places on nodes; a workload object with a replica count can also be used to keep a chosen number of containers running indefinitely. The effect is persistence that survives the deletion of any single pod, because the controller recreates whatever the declared state requires, and the code can land on nodes that the operator never logged in to. The evidence lives in the control plane: objects and their revisions in the cluster's key-value store, audit records naming the identity that created or changed a workload, controller events about scheduling and image pulls, and the image itself if it came from a registry the organisation does not control. The main differentiator from normal operations is provenance, since existing automation also creates jobs, so the review focuses on who created the object, which service account or namespace it runs in, which image it uses, and whether it was applied from a pipeline or typed in by hand.

beginner.definition: Container orchestration is software that runs many containers for you, and Kubernetes is the most common example. A container is a packaged program that runs the same way on any machine. This sub-technique is when an attacker creates a scheduled or repeating workload in that platform so their container keeps starting. It is part of the Scheduled Task/Job parent technique, but the timer here belongs to the cluster.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you delete a single container, the platform may simply create a new one. That makes an intrusion hard to remove by hand. An attacker with cluster rights can also reach every node the work is placed on, not just one server. The change may look like a normal deployment, so it can sit unnoticed for a long time.
howItWorks: The attacker gets access to the cluster, often through a stolen or over-permissive service account.
They create a scheduled workload object that points at a container image holding their program.
The platform controller notices the new object and starts one or more containers for it on chosen nodes.
If a container is deleted, the controller creates a replacement to match the declared state.
They may also set a replica count so a fixed number of containers always stay running.
The objects are recorded in the control plane with the identity that created them and the image used.
beginner.example: Think of a large office with an automated stationery service. You fill in a form for a delivery every Monday. A depot robot brings the box wherever it is told. If someone throws the box away, the robot brings another one next week. The form is still on file. The person who filed the form never has to visit the office again. Only the log of who submitted the form shows it was not a real employee request.
takeaways: Deleting a container is not enough when a controller keeps recreating it.
Review who created the workload object and which image it uses.
Cluster audit records are the main evidence, so protect and collect them.

objectives: Explain how scheduled and repeating workloads differ from a container started by hand.
Describe how a controller recreates containers to match a declared state and why that aids persistence.
Identify the control plane records that show who created a workload and from which image.
Explain the risk from over-permissive service accounts and how to bound their rights.
Compare a suspicious workload with legitimate pipeline automation using provenance and namespace.
